paragraphs: Inyene hannedarim haechad hem nidre tzedaqa o shear debar mitzva shel limmud vekayyotze vehashsheni hem nidre issur sheoser al atzmo debarim hammuttarim kegon shello yokal shello yashan shello yelek shello yedabber shello yehaneh vekayyotze bazeh shehem nedarim shel reshut vekol hannoder veeno meqayyem ober belav vaaseh diktib ish ki yiddor neder laAdonai o hishshaba shebua lesor issar al napsho lo yachel debaro kekol hayyotze mippiv yaaseh uketib motza sepateka tishmor veasita lepikak yizzaher haadam shello yadur shum neder shello yabo limol bahem. veameru chakamim hamacher nidro shello qiyyemu velo hittiru, hare zeh pinqaso niptachat umedaqdeqin bemaasayv im hem keday lehagen:

clarification.explanation: There are two types of vows. The first type is a vow of charity or to perform a commandment, such as studying a particular topic. The second type is a vow of prohibition, where a person forbids himself things otherwise permitted — such as not eating, not sleeping, not walking, not speaking, or not benefiting from something — these being voluntary vows. Anyone who vows and does not fulfill his vow transgresses both a negative and a positive commandment, as it is said that one who vows or swears shall not profane his word and shall do according to all that emerges from his mouth, and it is said, "that which emerges from your lips you shall keep and do." Therefore a person must be careful not to make any vow, so as not to come to violate and transgress it. Our Sages said that one who delays fulfilling his vow, neither fulfilling nor releasing it, has his ledger opened in Heaven, and his deeds are scrutinized to check whether they are worthy of protecting him.
takeaways: Two types of vows: vows of commandment/charity, and vows of prohibition on permitted things.
One who vows and does not fulfill transgresses a negative and a positive commandment.
It is better to avoid vows altogether, to avoid coming to violate them.
One who delays fulfilling his vow has his ledger opened in Heaven and his deeds scrutinized.

paragraphs: Hannoder bidbar hareshut im epshar lehattir nidro dehaynu sheyyesh lo petach lehattir veeno rotzeh lehattiro niqra rasha abal im lo matza petach lehattiro "p shemmeqayyemo niqra chote kol zeman shennaderu alayv bammeh debarim amurim benidre reshut abal nidre mitzva o nidre tzedaqa im kebar nadar az mitzva leqayyemam velo yishal hattara alehem ella middochaq mikkol maqom gam bazeh yizzaher lekattechilla shello yadur ella yaaseh hammitzva veyitten hatztzedaqa beli qabbalat shum neder mihu muttar liddor lekattechilla bidbar tzedaqa im kavvanato bazeh laasot laacherim veayyen shiyyure beraka siman r"g ot '.

clarification.explanation: One who makes a voluntary vow — if it is possible to have the vow released, that is, there is a legitimate opening to release it, and yet he does not wish to have it released — is called wicked. But if no opening is found to release his vow, even though he fulfills it, he is called a sinner as long as the vow remains upon him. This applies to voluntary vows. But vows of commandment or charity, once made, should be fulfilled, and one should not seek a release for them except in a pressing situation. Nevertheless, even with vows of commandment, one should as the primary practice be careful not to vow at all, but rather perform the commandment and give the charity without making any vow. Nevertheless, it is permitted as the primary practice to vow charity if his intent is to arouse and encourage others to give as well.
takeaways: One who makes a voluntary vow with an available opening for release and does not release it is called wicked.
Vows of commandment/charity, once made, should be fulfilled and not released except in a pressing situation.
As the primary practice, it is preferable to perform the commandment and give charity without a vow.
It is permitted to vow charity as the primary practice if intended to encourage others.

paragraphs: Keshehaadam betzara muttar liddor lekattechilla kediktib vayyiddar yaaqob neder lemor hora lanu sheyyidderu beet tzara veyesh omerim sheen leneder zeh hattara kelal ella tzarik leqayyemo uleinyan halaka yesh lehattir letzorek mitzva o bishbil tzorek gadol meod o heka deyadeinan beberur sheeno yakol leqayyem nidro veayyen chakemat adam vekatab haggaon chida" za"l beshiyyure beraka ap al gab deatta nahagu rabbim ladur lerabbi meir baal hannes o lishar tzaddiqim kede sheyyassigu dabar zeh o rivvach zeh, mikkol maqom tob litten hanneder bimzumman miqqodem sheyyassigu haddabar vekatab beshem hrm" za"l sheyyomar hannoder elaha demeiyyar aneni vikavven lekavvana shekkivven rabbi meir baal hannes bazeh beet sheamar lesar bet hassohar sheyyomar ken veyinnatzel (aboda zara dap k).

clarification.explanation: When a person is in distress, it is permitted for him to vow as the primary practice, since we find that our father Jacob vowed a vow at the time of his distress, teaching us that it is permitted to vow in a time of distress. Some say such a vow has no release at all and must be fulfilled, but halachically it may be released for the sake of a commandment, or for a very great need, or when it is clear the vower cannot fulfill his vow. The Chida wrote in Shiyurei Berachah that although many are accustomed to vow charity to Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes or other righteous figures so they will help them attain something or a profit, it is better to give the vowed sum in cash even before attaining what they seek. He further wrote in the name of the Ramo, that the vower should say "God of Meir, answer me," intending the same intention Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes had when he said this phrase, by whose merit he was saved.
takeaways: In a time of distress, it is permitted to vow as the primary practice, as Jacob did.
A vow made in distress should be released only for the sake of a commandment, a great need, or when it cannot be fulfilled.
One who vows to Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes should preferably give the money in cash in advance.
The formula for salvation: "God of Meir, answer me," with the intention of Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes.

paragraphs: Haomer eshneh halaka zo o eeseh dabar zeh vehu debar mitzva hare zeh neder vechayyab leqayyemo veim kol zeh yargil lomar al kol debar mitzva beli neder vaapillu mi shehaya zolel vesobe vekayyotze bazeh o sheddarko lehistakker beyeno ad sheyyabo biskaro lidbar nebelot ushear kiur demitztzad haddin mitzva laasot nedarim leesor hayyayin vehassakar alayv deal zeh ameru rabbotenu za"l nedarim seyag liprishut im kol zeh tob sheyyitgabber al yitzro liprosh miyyayin veshekar beli neder:

clarification.explanation: One who says "I will study this topic" or "I will do this thing" regarding a matter of commandment — his words are considered a vow and he must fulfill them. It is therefore proper to get into the habit of saying, for every commandment one undertakes, the addition "without a vow," so as not to become obligated. And by strict law, one accustomed to gluttony and drunkenness, or accustomed to becoming drunk on wine until he reaches vile and disgraceful speech from his drunkenness, is commanded to make a vow forbidding himself wine and beer, since our Sages said that vows are a fence for abstinence. Nevertheless, it is better for him to overcome his inclination and abstain from wine and beer without a vow.
takeaways: Saying "I will do this commandment" is considered a vow and must be fulfilled.
One should get into the habit of saying "without a vow" for every commandment undertaken.
One who has stumbled into drunkenness and vileness is, by strict law, commanded to vow against wine and beer.
It is preferable to overcome one's inclination and abstain from wine without a vow.

paragraphs: Lo yomar adam eddor umah bekak kesheertzeh elek veattayyarenu demikkol maqom hu neenash al mah shennadar vahare zeh domeh leadam shemmappil atzmo betzoa verotzeh sheyyirchatzu oto ugedole haacharonim katebu derauy liqnos hannoder beezeh dabar qodem sheyyattiru lo:

clarification.explanation: A person should not say to himself, "I will vow, and what of it, when I wish I will go and have the vow released" — since in any case he is punished for the very act of vowing, and he resembles a person who throws himself into filth expecting to be washed afterward. The great later authorities wrote that it is proper to impose some penalty on the vower even before releasing his vow, so he does not treat vows lightly.
takeaways: One should not say "I will vow and later release it," since one is punished for the very act of vowing.
One who vows intending to have it released resembles someone who soils himself expecting to be washed.
It is proper to impose a penalty on the vower before releasing his vow.

paragraphs: Hannoder ladur beeretz yisrael bazzeman hazzeh gam ken niqra neder mitzva veen mattirin lo ella middochaq vehu haddin benoder laalot lzyyr"h (biqqur hattitchut al qibre tzaddiqim) leeretz yisrael tvbb", nechshab neder mitzva. vehannoder lelek lehishtatteach al qibre hatztzaddiqim hare zeh neder vetzarik lo hattara:

clarification.explanation: One who vows to dwell in the Land of Israel in our time — his vow is considered a vow of commandment, and it is released only in a pressing situation. The same law applies to one who vows to go up and visit the graves of the righteous in the Land of Israel, which is likewise considered a vow of commandment. But one who vows to go and prostrate himself at the graves of the righteous — this is an ordinary vow requiring release.
takeaways: A vow to dwell in the Land of Israel in our time is a vow of commandment.
A vow to visit the graves of the righteous in the Land of Israel is likewise a vow of commandment.
A vow to prostrate oneself at the graves of the righteous is an ordinary vow requiring release.

paragraphs: Katub battora ish ki yiddor neder laAdonai veku' lesor issar al napsho lamedu rabbotenu za"l bah dehanneder haamur battora hu kegon sheyyomar kikkar zeh alay qarebban o keqarebban, veissar haamur hu kegon sheamur kikkar zeh asur alay o yeaser alay kikkar zeh vahare zeh asur alayv kediktib lesor issar al napsho veim amar yeaser yeni o peti o shear debarim al kol yisrael hare zeh sapeq im yakol leesor al acherim bilshon issur vehave zeh sepeqa deorayeta, veqayma lan lechumera. abal im amar qonam o qarebban kikkar zeh al kol yisrael yesh zeh issur min hattora lekulle alema. veayyen chakemat adam:

clarification.explanation: It is written in the Torah that a person vows a vow or forbids an oath-prohibition upon himself, and from this our Sages derived the distinction between a "neder" (vow) and an "issar" (prohibition). A "neder" is when a person ties the prohibition to something of sacrificial status, such as saying "this loaf is upon me as a sacrifice" or "like a sacrifice." An "issar" is when he forbids the item itself, such as saying "this loaf is forbidden to me," and it becomes forbidden to him. And if he said "my wine is forbidden" or "my bread is forbidden" regarding all of Israel, in the language of prohibition, it is a doubt whether he can forbid something on others with this language, and since this is a Torah-level doubt, one is stringent about it. But if he said "konam" or "this loaf is a sacrifice upon all of Israel," in sacrificial language, this is Torah-forbidden according to all opinions.
takeaways: A "neder" uses sacrificial language: "this loaf is upon me as a sacrifice."
An "issar" forbids the item itself: "this loaf is forbidden to me."
Forbidding others with prohibition-language is a Torah-level doubt, resolved stringently.
Forbidding others with sacrificial language is Torah-forbidden according to all.

paragraphs: Im haya lepanayv kikkar o dabar acher sheaseru alayv beneder o beissur kaamur veamar al kikkar acher yihyeh zeh kazeh hare zeh neesar alayv veken hu haddin im hayu lepanayv kikkar vekayyotze shenneesar al acherim mippene sheasaruhu al atzman vezeh hitpis bo sheamar dabar zeh yihyeh kazeh hare zeh neesar bekak:

clarification.explanation: If he had before him a loaf or another item he had already forbidden himself by vow or prohibition, and said of another loaf "let this be like that one," the second loaf becomes forbidden to him, since he tied it to something already vowed. The same law applies if there was before him a loaf and the like forbidden to others because they had forbidden it to themselves, and he came and tied his words to them, saying "let this thing be like that one" — the second item likewise becomes forbidden to him.
takeaways: One who ties an item to something already vowed forbids the second item too.
Saying "let this be like that" casts the prohibition onto the new item.
One can also tie to an item forbidden to others by their own vow.

paragraphs: Im hayu mebaqqeshim mimmennu leekol veamar yihyeh besar chazir im okal o yihyeh dam chazir im okal hare zeh asur midderabbanan ad sheyyattiru lo demin hattora en nitpas beneder ella ad sheyyatpis bedabar hannadur abal im hitpis bedabar haasur mitztzad atzmo belav haki eno nitpas ella midderabbanan umihu im amar kikkar zeh asur alay kibsar chazir yesh omerim dehave neder middeorayta shehare im lo siyyem kibsar chazir haya asur min hattora bevadday mippene sheamar bilshono asur veayyen chakemat adam:

clarification.explanation: If asked to eat, and he said "let it be like pig meat if I eat" or "let it be like pig blood if I eat," this is forbidden to him only rabbinically until it is released for him. The reason is that by Torah law a vow takes effect only when tied to something already vowed, that is, something forbidden by vow; but if he tied it to something forbidden in its own right, like pig meat, this is not a Torah-level vow, only rabbinic. Nevertheless, if he said "this loaf is forbidden to me like pig meat," some say this is a Torah-level vow, since even without adding "like pig meat" it would have been Torah-forbidden because he used the language "forbidden."
takeaways: Tying to something forbidden in its own right (like pig meat) forbids only rabbinically.
By Torah law, a vow takes effect only by tying to something already vowed.
If he opened with the language "forbidden to me," some say it is Torah-forbidden.

paragraphs: Adam oser al atzmo dabar shello ba, liksheyyabo laolam. abal al chabero eno yakol leesor dabar shello ba laolam veayyen sha"k siman r"h seip qatan t"v:

clarification.explanation: A person can forbid himself by vow even something that has not yet come into existence, and the prohibition takes effect when it comes into existence. But regarding his fellow, a person cannot forbid something that has not yet come into existence.
takeaways: A person can vow-forbid himself something not yet existing; the prohibition takes effect when it comes to exist.
One cannot forbid his fellow something not yet existing.

paragraphs: "g deim amar lachabero ani noder shello okal o sheokal immeka en zeh leshon neder kelal dela asar haakila al atzmo ella neder al gupo sheyyokal o lo yokal velashon zeh hu shayyak beshabua sheyyomar ani nishba shello okal immeka o sheokal immeka abal leshon neder hu tzarik leesor hachepetz al atzmo mikkol maqom kevan dehaiddana margela bepummayhu deinashe lemineddar behay lishshana en lehaqel veim amar ken asur ad sheyyattiru lo;

clarification.explanation: If a person said to his fellow, "I vow that I will not eat with you" or "that I will eat with you," by strict law this is not vow-language at all, since he did not forbid the eating itself as an object, but spoke of his own body eating or not eating — and this language belongs specifically to an oath, which takes effect on the body. True vow-language must forbid the object itself. Nevertheless, since in our time people are accustomed to vow with this language, one should not be lenient, and if he said so, it is forbidden until released.
takeaways: "I vow not to eat with you" is oath-language, not vow-language.
A true vow forbids the object itself; an oath takes effect on the body.
Since people commonly use this language, one should not be lenient — it is forbidden until released.

paragraphs: Haomer leishto titasseri alay hare zeh neeseret alayv vetzarik hattara kishar nedarim abal haomer ishti asura alay eno kelum veim emor meatta umeakshav asura alay hare zo asura vetzarik hattara al nidro vekol shekken im hosip veamar veeni rotzeh bachabertah deneeseret vetzarik hattara veayyen keneset haggedola siman r"h haggahat hattur ot b':

clarification.explanation: One who says to his wife, "you shall become forbidden to me," forbids her and requires release like other vows, since the language speaks of the future. But one who says "my wife is forbidden to me" in the past or plain present tense — this accomplishes nothing. And if he said "from now on she is forbidden to me," she becomes forbidden and his vow requires release. All the more so if he added, "and I do not want her company," she becomes forbidden and requires release.
takeaways: "You shall become forbidden to me" forbids the wife and requires release.
"My wife is forbidden to me" plainly accomplishes nothing.
"From now on she is forbidden to me" forbids and requires release.

paragraphs: En hanneder chal ad sheyyotziu bispatayv veyihyu piv velibbo shavin lepikak haya belibbo liddor mippat chittim vehotzi bepiv pat seorim muttar bishnehem abal haya belibbo pat chittim vehotzi pat setam asur beshel chittim lebad mippene sheppiv eno makchish mah shebbilbabo degam pat chittim niqra pat setam:

clarification.explanation: A vow takes effect only when the person utters it with his lips, and his mouth and heart must agree — that thought and speech coincide. Therefore if he intended in his heart to vow regarding wheat bread but mistakenly uttered "barley bread," both are permitted, since his mouth and heart do not agree. But if he intended wheat bread in his heart and uttered plain "bread," wheat bread is forbidden, since his mouth does not contradict what is in his heart — wheat bread too is included in plain "bread."
takeaways: A vow takes effect only when uttered with agreement between mouth and heart.
Intending wheat but uttering barley — both are permitted.
Intending wheat and uttering plain "bread" — wheat is forbidden, since the mouth does not contradict the heart.

paragraphs: Neder o shebua shello hotziam bepiv ella hem ketubim bishtar hodaa vechatam bashshetar - en bahem mammash veyesh machmirin bazeh venakon lachush ledibrehem veayyen keneset haggedola siman r"y haggahat hattur ot v':

clarification.explanation: A vow or oath a person did not utter with his mouth, but only wrote in a document and signed, has no substance and does not take effect, since he did not utter it with his lips. Some are stricter, holding that such writing also obligates, and it is proper to be concerned for their view.
takeaways: A vow/oath only written, not spoken, has no substance.
Some are stricter, holding writing also obligates — proper to be concerned for this view.

paragraphs: Hannoder o nishba bachalom eno kelum deen kan lo peh velo leb veyesh omerim detzarik hattara veadderabba kevan demin hashshamayim hiddiruhu la saggi behattara bishlosha ella bae hattara baasara bene adam deyadei lemiqre vetzarik lachush ledibrehem lehattir baasara deyadei lemiqre veraq im lo nimtza lo asara ellu benaqel la matrechinan leh veyattiru lo bishlosha kishar neder vetzarik sheyyattiru lo bacharata keillu nadar behaqitz vaapillu im raa shennadar o nishba bachalom veraa name bachalom shehittiru lo gam zeh tzarik sheyyattiru lo behaqitz veken ishsha shennadera bachalom tzerika hattara baasara kemo haish veen habbaal yakol lehaper lah apillu shehu neder middebarim dimhanne bah hapara ella tzerika hattara baasara vaapillu im adam acher raa bachalom al ish o al haishsha shennaderu o nishbeu bachalom tzerikin hattara baasara keillu hem rau bachalom al atzman ukemo shekkatab btshb"tz cheleq b' siman qs"ch veken hebi beseper yedot nedarim mehashsheiltot yeuyyan sham:

clarification.explanation: One who vows or swears within a dream has nothing, since there is neither mouth nor heart there. Some say it requires release, and moreover, since it was imposed from Heaven, three are not sufficient for the release, but release requires ten literate people. One should be concerned for this view and release it with ten literate people, and only if ten such people are not readily found should one not trouble oneself, releasing it with three like an ordinary vow. The release is done through remorse, as though he had vowed while awake. Even if he saw in his dream both that he vowed and that it was released for him, he still requires release while awake. Likewise, a woman who vowed in a dream requires release by ten just like a man, and her husband cannot annul it for her — she requires release by ten. And even if another person saw in his dream that a man or woman vowed, they require release by ten as though they themselves had seen it in their own dream.
takeaways: A dream-vow is by strict law nothing, since there is no mouth or heart.
Some require release by ten literate people; if unavailable, three suffice with remorse.
A woman's dream-vow also requires release by ten — her husband cannot annul it.

paragraphs: Hannoder o nishba vechozer meatzmo tok kede dibbur dehaynu shiur sheyyomar shalom aleka rabbi im peresh chazarato bepiv apillu sheamar belachash shello hishmia ella leazenayv bilbad hare zeh nidro ushebuato betelin veen tzarik lahem hattara abal im chashab bilbabo hachazara la mehanne "p shechashab tok kede dibbur didbarim shebballeb enam debarim lebattel mah shemmotzi bepiv meachar ki kaasher hotzi hanneder o hashshebua bepiv hayu piv velibbo shavin:

clarification.explanation: One who vows or swears and retracts on his own within the time it takes to speak — that is, the brief time in which one says "peace upon you, my teacher" — if he explicitly stated his retraction with his mouth, even in a whisper only he himself heard, the vow and oath are void and require no release. But if he only thought in his heart to retract without uttering it with his lips, the retraction does not help, even though he thought it within that brief time, since matters of the heart are not considered words and cannot nullify what he already uttered when his mouth and heart agreed.
takeaways: Retracting a vow verbally within "the time of speech" voids it without release.
"The time of speech" is the measure of saying "peace upon you, my teacher."
Retracting only in thought, without speech, does not help.

paragraphs: Harotzeh linhog lehitannot beereb rosh chodesh o bime hashshobabim o beyamim noraim yomar bepiv beperush qodem minhago sheeno meqabbel alayv zeh beneder velo betorat minhag leolam ella raq beet sheyyirtzeh lehitannot yeqabbel hattaanit qodem mibbeod yom veim lo yirtzeh lehitannot apillu sheen lo sibba monaat vehekrechit rashshay hu shello yitanneh velo yeqabbel alayv hattaanit mibbeod yom kaka yomar beperush qodem sheyyatchil linhog veim hu nahag bistam velo hitna bekak beperush veachare zeh rotzeh laazob minhago mechamat chalishut gupo o sibba acheret yaaseh hattara veyiptach bacharata shemmitcharet al hamminhag shennahag bistam velo peresh sheyyihyeh beli neder abal lo yihyeh mitcharet al qabbalat taaniyyot sheqqibbel vehitanna qodem denimtza toheh al harishonot ella raq mitcharet al qabbalat hamminhag bilshon setam shello hitna beperush sheyyehe beli neder vekaasher timtza katub benosach hattarat nedarim beameram en anachnu tohim veku' ella anachnu mitcharetim al qabbalat hainyanim bilshon neder veku' velo amarnu hinneh anachnu osim zeh beli neder veku': veotam hannohagim issur bidbarim hammuttarim mechamat shessoberim shehem asurim veatta nitbarer shehem muttarim hare zeh neder betaut veeno kelum vaapillu im hayu soberim shehu issur gadol veaach"k nitbarer lahem shehu chumera bealema la chashib neder:

clarification.explanation: One who wishes to adopt the practice of fasting on the eve of Rosh Chodesh, during the Shovavim days, or during the Days of Awe, should explicitly state before beginning his practice that he does not accept this as a vow nor as a permanent practice forever, but only that each time he wishes to fast, he will accept the fast the day before, and if he does not wish to fast, even without a preventing reason, he may choose not to fast and not accept it. This condition should be stated explicitly before beginning the practice. And if he practiced plainly without conditioning, and afterward wants to abandon the practice due to bodily weakness or another reason, he should perform a release. In the release, he should begin with remorse over the very acceptance of the practice plainly without conditioning it to be without a vow, but should not regret the fasts he already accepted and observed, so as not to regret commandments already performed. Likewise, one who was accustomed to be stringent regarding permitted things by mistake, thinking them forbidden, and it later became clear they are permitted — this is a mistaken vow and is nothing. Even if he thought it a great prohibition and it later turned out to be merely a stringency, this is not considered a vow.
takeaways: One wishing to adopt fasting practices should explicitly condition that it is not a vow nor a permanent practice.
One who practiced plainly and wants to stop needs release with remorse over the acceptance itself, not over fasts already kept.
A stringency adopted by mistake, later found unnecessary, is not a vow at all.

paragraphs: Shebua chala min hattora apillu al dabar sheen bo mammashut kegon shena vedibbur ushemia verecha vekayyotze abal nedarim enam chalim min hattora ella al dabar sheyyesh bo mammash ak midderabbanan gam hannedarim chalim al dabar sheen bo mammash. lepikak haoser alayv lishmoa tepillat shimon hare zeh asur midderabbanan ad sheyyaaseh hattara veim amar qonam pi medabber immak qonam yaday osot immak qonam ragli lahalok veenay lishon vekayyotze bazeh have neder min hattora shehare hizkir haebarim sheyyesh bahem mammash:

clarification.explanation: An oath takes effect by Torah law even on something with no substance, such as sleep, speech, hearing, or smell. But vows take effect by Torah law only on something with substance, like an object, and only rabbinically do vows also take effect on something without substance. Therefore one who forbids himself from hearing so-and-so's prayer is forbidden only rabbinically until released, since hearing has no substance. But if he said "konam my mouth speaking with you," "konam my hands working with you," "konam my feet from walking," or "my eyes from sleeping," this is a Torah-level vow, since he mentioned the limbs themselves, which have substance.
takeaways: An oath takes effect by Torah law even on something insubstantial, like sleep and speech.
A vow takes effect by Torah law only on something substantial; rabbinically also on the insubstantial.
Vowing regarding hearing is only rabbinically forbidden.
Vowing on limbs (mouth, hands, feet, eyes) is Torah-level.

paragraphs: Hannedarim chalim gam al debar mitzva abal hashshebua enah chala al debar mitzva mippene shehashshebua hi al gup haadam velo al hachepetz ukebar gup haadam mushba veomed mehar sinay leqayyem hammitzva lepikak hannishba lebattel dabar hamporash battora kegon tzitzit utepillin umatztza vekayyotze bazeh hare zeh loqeh al shebuato mippene shehi shebuat shave umeqayyem hammitzva hahi. bammeh debarim amurim benishba al mitzva bilchudeh, kegon shennishba shello yokal matztza belel pesach abal im kolel gam debarim hammuttarim kegon shennishba shello yokal matztza setam miggo dechala al shear yemot hashshana chala name al hammatztza delel pesach:

clarification.explanation: Vows take effect even on a matter of commandment, since they forbid the object. But an oath does not take effect on a matter of commandment, since it takes effect on the person's body, and the body is already under oath from Mount Sinai to fulfill the commandments, and an oath cannot take effect on an oath. Therefore one who swears to nullify something explicit in the Torah, such as tzitzit, tefillin, or matzah, is lashed for his oath since it is a vain oath, and he still fulfills the commandment. This applies specifically when he swore regarding the commandment alone, such as swearing not to eat matzah on Passover night. But if his oath also included permitted things, such as swearing not to eat matzah at all during the entire year, since the oath takes effect on the rest of the year's days when matzah is optional, it takes effect on the matzah of Passover night too.
takeaways: A vow takes effect on a matter of commandment, but an oath does not.
The body is already under oath from Sinai — an oath cannot take effect on an oath.
One who swears to nullify an explicit commandment is lashed for a vain oath but still fulfills the commandment.
An oath including permitted things too takes effect on the commandment as well.

paragraphs: Hannishba al debar mitzva shehu midderabbanan, kegon shello lehadliq ner chanukka, o shello liqrot hammegilla - chala hashshebua. veken im nishba leqayyem metzuvveh shehi midderabbanan, umebattelah - chayyab mishshum shebua. vehu haddin ledabar shehu midrash chakamim sheeno meporash battora; vehaynu tamah mishshum dishbua zo shennishba atta, hachiyyub shellah meporash battora, velaqach hi allima vachazaqa, sheyyekola lachul al dabar shehu qalush veqal maneh. bammeh debarim amurim? benishba al midderabbanan besheb veal taaseh, o shennishba laasot uleqayyem metzuvveh midderabbanan, deallume alma limtzuvva, abal im nishba laabor al mitzvat lo taaseh derabbanan – lo chala zo hashshebua, mippene shehu ober al lo taaseh derabbanan beyadayim bequm vaaseh, ukebar hu mushba veomed mehar sinay belav d"l tasur" (debarim yz,y); mikkol maqom, tob sheyyishal al shebbiuto.

clarification.explanation: One who swears regarding a matter of rabbinic commandment, such as not to light Chanukah candles or not to read the Megillah, the oath takes effect. Likewise, one who swore to fulfill a rabbinic commandment and later nullified it, he is liable for the oath. The reason is that the obligation of this oath is explicit in the Torah, and it is strong enough to take effect even on a light, rabbinic matter. This applies to one who swore regarding a rabbinic commandment in a passive manner (not to do something), or swore to arise and perform a rabbinic commandment, where the oath strengthens the commandment. But if he swore to actively transgress a rabbinic negative commandment, the oath does not take effect, since he is already under oath from Sinai regarding the prohibition of "you shall not deviate." Nevertheless, it is good for him to seek release for his oath.
takeaways: An oath regarding a rabbinic commandment takes effect.
The oath's obligation is explicit in the Torah, strong enough for even a light, rabbinic matter.
An oath to actively transgress a rabbinic prohibition does not take effect, due to "you shall not deviate."
It is still good to seek release for such an oath.

paragraphs: Im nishba laabor al lo taaseh derabbanan bekolel debarim hammuttarim im haasurim - yesh omerim dehashshebua chala, umikkol maqom kopin oto lehattir shebuato velo yaabor:

clarification.explanation: If he swore to transgress a rabbinic negative commandment, but included in his oath permitted things together with the forbidden ones, some say the oath takes effect since it takes effect on the permitted things. Nevertheless, he is compelled to have his oath released so he does not transgress the prohibition.
takeaways: An oath to transgress a rabbinic prohibition, including permitted things too, some say takes effect.
He is compelled to release his oath so as not to transgress the prohibition.

paragraphs: En shebua chala al shebua ketzad amar shebua shello okal kikkar zeh vechazar veamar shebua shello okal kikkar zeh en hashsheniyya chala kelal shehare hu kebar mushba alayv vahare hu alayv kishar issure tora vedavqa bishbua dilhabba, hu deen chala hashsheniyya dehave kenishba leqayyem hammitzva abal bishbua shellaubbar kegon sheamar shebua shello akalti hayyom vechazar veamar shebua shello akalti hayyom yesh kan onesh shene shabuot lashsheqer detekep keshennishba shebua rishona yatzea mippiv lashsheqer vehaleka lah vehashsheniyya hi shebua chadasha bipne atzmah: veha deamerinan en shebua chala al shebua dilhabba im hittiru al harishona chala hashsheniyya dehechakam oqer behattara et hashshebua harishona ukeillu lo haya shebua rishona lepikak im nishba al dabar echad shene peamim o yoter mattirin lo techilla harishona veaach"k tachul hashsheniyya meeleha velaken mattirin lo od paam shenit veken al zo hadderek demattirin lo kol kak peamim kepi mispar hashshabuot shennishba al ken zeh shebba lishol al shebuato im yodea kamma peamim nishba al oto dabar yaggid lehammattirim kede sheyyattiru lo keneged hashshabuot shennishba vbsh"q mqbtzyl amarti laken tiqqenu bilshon hattara shelosh peamim muttarim leka veshalosh peamim mechullim leka veshalosh peamim sheraveyan leka "g debachada saggi vehaynu ki shemma yatza mippiv shenayim veshalosh peamim shebuot al oto dabar velav addateh dimhanne leh hakkepel demuttarim umecholim vesheraveyin keillu asu lo shelosha hattarot bezeh achar zeh:

clarification.explanation: An oath does not take effect on an oath. How so: if he said "an oath that I will not eat this loaf" and again said "an oath that I will not eat this loaf," the second oath does not take effect at all, since he is already under oath about it and the loaf is upon him like other Torah prohibitions. This applies specifically to an oath about the future, but for an oath about the past, such as saying "an oath that I did not eat today" and repeating it, there is a penalty for two false oaths, since already with the first oath he uttered a falsehood, and the second is a new oath in its own right. And what we said about an oath not taking effect on an oath regarding the future — if the first was released, the second takes effect, since the sage's release uproots the first oath as though it never existed. Therefore if he swore about the same thing twice or more, the first is released first, and then the second takes effect on its own, and they release him again according to the number of oaths he swore. Therefore one who comes to inquire about his oath, if he knows how many times he swore about the same thing, should tell this to those releasing him, so they release against all his oaths. For this reason it was instituted to say in the release formula three times "released for you," three times "forgiven for you," and three times "absolved for you," to also cover a case where he swore twice or three times about the same thing without noticing.
takeaways: An oath does not take effect on an oath regarding the future.
For a false oath about the past, there is a penalty for each oath separately.
If the first is released, the second takes effect, so release is repeated per the number of oaths.
The triple release formula covers unnoticed repeated oaths.

paragraphs: Neder chal al neder ketzad amar kikkar zeh asur alay vechazar veamar kikkar zeh asur alay shenehem chalin veim akalo chayyab shenayim vehattaam mishshum dindarim chal haissur al hachepetz velaken chal alayv apillu mea peamim:

clarification.explanation: A vow takes effect on a vow. How so: if he said "this loaf is forbidden to me" and repeated "this loaf is forbidden to me," both vows take effect, and if he ate the loaf he is liable twice for it. The reason is that with vows the prohibition takes effect on the object itself, and therefore it can take effect on it even a hundred times, unlike an oath, which takes effect on the body, where an oath does not take effect on an oath.
takeaways: A vow takes effect on a vow, and eating incurs double liability.
With vows, the prohibition takes effect on the object, so it can take effect even a hundred times.
This differs from an oath, which takes effect on the body and does not take effect on an oath.

paragraphs: Qibbelu chaza"l mi shennadar venitcharet yesh lo taqqana "y hattara sheyyattiru lo nidro vehu haddin lishbua dimhanne hattara apillu nishba behazkarat hashshem ak en mattirin lishbua ella middochaq o letzorek mitzva mippene shehaggeonim hayu machmirim harbeh bizmannam bishbuot veayyen birke yosep simanim r"l vrl"d, veen mattirim bazzeman hazzeh pachot mishshelosha bene adam vaapillu shehem hedyotot sheenam mumchim saggi, abal mikkol maqom lo yihyu amme haaretz ella lepachot yihyu bemadrega zo digmir lehu vesaberi dehaynu sheim melammedim otam halakot hem mebinim "p shehem enam yekolim lehabin meatzman. veim lo hittiru lo shelosha apillu hittiru lo shenayim chakamim gedolim en hattaratan kelum:

clarification.explanation: Our Sages accepted that one who vows and regrets has a remedy through release, whereby his vow is released for him, and likewise an oath, for which release is likewise effective, even one sworn by mentioning God's name. However, an oath is released only in a pressing situation or for the sake of a commandment, since the Geonim were very stringent about oaths in their time. A vow or oath is released only by no fewer than three people, and even ordinary laymen who are not experts suffice — though they should at least not be complete ignoramuses, but at a level where, if taught the laws, they understand, even though they cannot understand on their own. And if only two, even great sages, released it rather than three, their release is nothing.
takeaways: One who vows or swears and regrets has a remedy through release, even for an oath by God's name.
An oath is released only in a pressing situation or for a commandment.
Release requires no fewer than three people, even laymen (not complete ignoramuses).
A release by only two, even great sages, is nothing.

paragraphs: "g demitztzad haddin im yomru paam achat muttar leka saggi nohagin lomar shelosh peamim muttar leka lechazzeq hainyan vehaiddana nahagu lomar shelosh peamim muttar leka veshalosh peamim machul leka veshalosh peamim sharuy leka vikolim lehattir bekol lashon sheyyihyeh mashmauto bilshon hattara hannizkeret vegam yekolim lehattir shenayim o shelosha nedarim beyachad lomar lo muttarim leka veken mattirim lishnayim o lishlosha anashim beyachad lomar lahem muttarim lakem:

clarification.explanation: Although by strict law it suffices for those releasing to say once "released for you," the custom is to say three times "released for you," to strengthen the matter. And today the custom is to say three times "released for you," three times "forgiven for you," and three times "absolved for you." Those releasing may release using any language whose meaning is release. Likewise, they may release two or three vows together, saying "released for you," and likewise release two or three people together, saying "released for you (plural)."
takeaways: By strict law one utterance suffices; the custom is three times, in triple formula.
Release may be in any language meaning release.
Multiple vows or multiple people may be released together.

paragraphs: Mattirim apillu qerobim v"g dekol dabar shetztzarik bet din en danin qerobim haka shari dela din hu abal nashim uqetannim en reuyim lehattir nedarim umi shehu ben y"g shana im lo nitbarer lanu shehebi shette searot la samekinan achazaqa deraba vetzarik bediqa leda im hebi shette searot deaz kasher lehattir veal ken nizharim shello liqqach mattirim ella raq anashim shennitmalle zeqanam veayin pitche teshuba beshem rama" za"l:

clarification.explanation: Vows are released even when those releasing are the vower's relatives, and although in any matter requiring a court, relatives do not judge, here it is permitted since this is not an actual legal judgment. But women and minors are not fit to release vows. And one who is thirteen years old, if it has not been established that he has produced two hairs evidencing his maturity, one does not rely on the presumption that he has produced them, and an examination is required to know if he has produced two hairs, at which point he is fit to release. Therefore care is taken to select only bearded, mature men as those who release.
takeaways: Vows may be released even by relatives, since this is not an actual legal judgment.
Women and minors are unfit to release vows.
A thirteen-year-old requires verification of maturity signs, not mere presumption.
Care is taken to select only bearded, mature men as releasers.

paragraphs: Mattirim apillu ballayla vaapillu beshabbat vaapillu shehaya yakol lehattir meetmol v"g deen danin beshabbat veen danim ballayla hay lav din hu mihu keshemmattirim beshabbat lo yattiru ella dabar shehu tzorek shabbat kegon shennadar shello yokal verotzeh leekol atta vekayyotze bazeh veraq nidre tzibbur nahagu lehattir beshabbat "p sheenah letzorek shabbat mippene shebbeshabbat kullam niqbatzim ubaim veim lo yattiru beyom zeh en yekolim lehattir bechol dela atu veim mattirim "y charata deen tzarik yishshub haddaat tepe yekolim lehattir meummad abal neder shetztzarik limtzo lo petach mishshum deeno mitcharet bo en muttarim ella meyushshab:

clarification.explanation: Vows are released even at night, even on the Sabbath, and even when he could have released it already the day before, and although judgment is not conducted on the Sabbath or at night, here it is permitted since this is not an actual legal judgment. However, when releasing on the Sabbath, only something needed for the Sabbath itself should be released, such as one who vowed not to eat and now wishes to eat. Only communal vows were customarily released on the Sabbath even when not needed for the Sabbath, since on the Sabbath everyone gathers, and if not released on that day, they could not be released on a weekday since people would not come. And if released through remorse, which does not require much deliberation, they may release even while those releasing are standing. But a vow requiring an "opening" to be found, since the vower does not regret it, is released only while those releasing are seated.
takeaways: Vows are released even at night and on the Sabbath, since this is not an actual legal judgment.
On the Sabbath, only something needed for the Sabbath itself should be released.
Communal vows are released on the Sabbath even without Sabbath need, since everyone gathers then.
Release through remorse can be done standing; release through an "opening" requires the releasers to be seated.

paragraphs: Tzarik hannoder o hannishba labo beatzmo lipne hammattirim vela mehanne "y shalicha veken name im katab biktab yado shemmitcharet la mehanne veim hammattirim en mebinim leshono kevan shehu atzmo omed lipne hammattirim yekolim lishmoa debaro min hamturgeman gam tzarik sheyyaggid haddabar shehu shoel alayv hattara lehammattirim mihu im gilla raq leechad mehem saggi:

clarification.explanation: The vower or swearer must come himself before those releasing, and release does not work through an agent. Likewise, if he only wrote in his own handwriting that he regrets it, this does not help. And if those releasing do not understand his language, since he himself stands before them, they may hear his words through a translator. He must state to those releasing the matter for which he seeks release, but if he revealed it to only one of them, this suffices.
takeaways: The vower must come himself before the releasers — no release through an agent.
A written statement of regret in his own hand does not help.
If they do not understand his language, they may hear him through a translator.
It suffices to reveal the matter to only one of the releasers.

paragraphs: Hanneder vehashshebua nittarim "y shene debarim haechad im mitcharet beiqqar hanneder vehashshebua shehaya rotzeh shello nadar velo nishba meiqqara, sheomer bepiv halvay shello nadarti velo nishbati veim beemet hu mitcharet charata gemura hare zeh mattirim lo bacharata zo abal im hu eno mitcharet al iqqar hanneder veatta yesh lo ratzon bishbua o beneder sheasa veraq mitcharet al zeman habba meatta umeakshav deen lo ratzon beneder mikkan ulehabba en moil lo hattara kelal vahare hu beissur neder kol yamayv v"p sheomer bepiv shehu mitcharet meiqqara lo yoil kelum: veopen hashsheni hu - im nitchaddesh lo atta sibba shemmechamatah rotzeh lebattel hanneder kegon shennadar lehitannot veatta roeh atzmo chalush meod dechulshato negdit leqiyyum hanneder o sheatta maptzirim bo bene adam sheyyattir et hanneder velo yinhog bo mikkan ulehabba vehu eno yakol lehashib penehem umukrach laasot retzonam "g dacharata zo enah kelum veen yekolim lehattir al yadah meachar deeno mitcharet gam al heabar meiqqar hanneder mikkol maqom toil charata zo laasot mimmenna petach vekak omerim lo hammattirim illu hayita yodea beet shennadarta shello tihyeh bari aach"k veyihyeh leka sibba monaat shehi negdiyt leneder o illu hayita yodea sheyyaptziru beka bene adam lehattir hanneder velo tukal lehashib penehem kelum hayita noder vehu meshib illu hayiti yodea kak lo hayiti noder hare zeh mattirin lo mippene shebbazeh nimtza haya nidro betaut veneeqar mimmela meiqqara veen zeh chashib nolad deqayma lan en potechin benolad yaan ki zeh hu dabar shekicha ulehaki mehanne petach zeh shehu petach mittok charata veraq tzerikin lizzaher shello laasot petach bedabar dela shekicha: vehinneh beittah bazzeman hazzeh nahagu laasot lekol nedarim ushebuot petach mittok charata yaan en somekim al hacharata apillu im omer shemmitcharet meiqqar hanneder dechosheshim ulay lo ken hu beemet vegam bepetach lechudeh lo nahagu mippene sheyyesh chilluqe dinim harbeh bimtziut happetach sheyyesh kamma debarim sheen potechin bahem velaken nohagim laasot petach mittok charata ditchilla shoalin oto im mitcharet meiqqara ukesheomer shemmitcharet meiqqara az omerim lo illu hayita yodea beshaa shennadarta shettitcharet lebassop kelum hayita noder vehu meshib lo ubazeh nimtza deneeqar hanneder meiqqara shennaasa betaut shehare apillu im timtze lemor sheeno mitcharet ella meakshav mikkol maqom neeqar hanneder mimmela shehare anachnu mattirin lo akshav "y petach velaken en chashash gam im hu mitcharet mechamat nolad dela shekicha yaan kevan dehu mitcharet mechamat hannolad veomer deillu yada bazeh lo haya noder day bekak veayyen chakemat adam kelal q' seip Adonai yeuyyan sham:

clarification.explanation: A vow and oath are released in two ways. The first, remorse, where the vower regrets the vow itself and is distressed that he vowed in the first place, saying with his mouth, "if only I had not vowed or sworn." And if he truly regrets completely, he is released on this basis. But if he does not regret the vow itself and still wants it, only he does not want it from now on, the release does not help at all, and he remains under the prohibition of his vow, even if he says with his mouth that he regrets it from the outset — this will not help. The second way, an "opening," where a new reason has arisen for which he wants to nullify the vow, such as one who vowed to fast and now finds himself weak, or people pressuring him to nullify the vow and he cannot refuse them. Although this new reason is not remorse over the past, nevertheless an "opening" is made from it, and those releasing say to him: had you known at the time of the vow that you would reach this weakness or that they would pressure you, would you have vowed — and he answers that he would not have vowed, so his vow was made in error and is uprooted from the outset. One might wonder, since the rule is "one does not open with something newly arisen" — that is, one does not make an opening for release by force of a reason that arose and newly developed only after the vow, since at the time of the vow it did not yet exist. But here release is granted nonetheless, since bodily weakness or social pressure are common and frequent things that every vower should anticipate in advance, and are therefore not considered a disqualifying "newly arisen" thing but a reason on which an opening can be built; therefore one must be careful not to make an opening from a new reason that is rare and uncommon, for which indeed one does not open. Today the custom is to make an opening from remorse together for all vows and oaths, since one does not rely on remorse alone, lest he not truly regret, nor on the opening alone, since it has many distinctions in law. Therefore they first ask him if he regrets from the outset, and when he says yes, they say to him: had you known at the time of the vow that you would end up regretting it, would you have vowed — and he answers no, and thereby the vow is uprooted from the outset as though made in error.
takeaways: A vow is released through remorse over the vow itself, or through an "opening" from a new reason.
Remorse only about the future does not help — remorse must be about the vow itself.
The opening: "had you known this would happen, would you have vowed" — leading to an error finding.
The rule is one does not open with a newly-arisen reason, but common things like weakness or social pressure are not disqualified as "newly arisen."
One should be careful not to build an opening on a rare, uncommon new reason.
Today, both remorse and an opening are used together, since neither alone is relied upon fully.

paragraphs: Hacherem vehannidduy "g ditzrikin hattara en tzerikin lo petach velo charata qodem hattara velaken im qibbel alayv ezeh dabar laasot o shello laasot sheqqibbelu becherem venidduy mattirin lo mihu hamnaddeh atzmo baolam habba im yaaseh kak katab maran za"l besiman rk"ch yesh mi sheomer sheyyesh lo hattara veyesh mi sheomer sheen lo hattara vekatab mvr"m za"l debimqom mitzva mattirin yeuyyan sham veyadua mah sheheelu happoseqim dedaat maran za"l lipsoq kisbara haacharona vekatab haggaon chida" za"l b"chayyim shaal" cheleq ' siman " ot g' dedaat haacharonim lehachmir benidduy olam habba, kaasher ala bqb"tz harab keneset haggedola siman rp"ch vehammeqillim lehattir haynu bimqom mitzva kemo shekkatab mvr"m veku' ubeniddon didan en lachush mitztzad nidduy olam habba dekatebu hattosapot vesiatam upasequ maran siman shl"d deim hattenay bedabar sheyyukal leqayyemo veqiyyemo - lo chal hannidduy veken katab haradba"z veku' yeuyyan sham vbsh"q rab pealim bitshuba heerakti beinyan zeh ubemah sheyyesh lechalleq ben nidduy lecherem udebarim hammistaapim bazeh vetzidde hahetter bazeh leadam sheamar kak yeuyyan sham vei epshar leparesh kan mippene haarikut:

clarification.explanation: A ban (cherem) and excommunication (nidui), although they require release, require neither an opening nor remorse before release, but are released directly. Therefore if a person undertook to do or not do something and accepted it under ban and excommunication, it is released for him. However, one who excommunicated himself regarding the World to Come if he does a certain thing — the authorities disagree whether he has a release. Maran cited that some say he has a release and some say he does not, and the Rema wrote that for the sake of a commandment, it is released. The Chida wrote that the later authorities' view is to be stringent regarding excommunication of the World to Come, being lenient to release only for the sake of a commandment. But in the case before us, there is no need for concern about excommunication of the World to Come, since the Tosafot and authorities wrote that if he conditioned it on something he could fulfill and fulfilled the condition, the excommunication does not take effect. The author of the Ben Ish Chai notes he elaborated on this matter in his book Rav Pe'alim, on the distinction between excommunication and a ban and the aspects of leniency.
takeaways: A ban and excommunication require release but need neither an opening nor remorse.
One who excommunicated himself regarding the World to Come — disputed whether release is possible; lenient only for a commandment.
If conditioned on something fulfillable and fulfilled, the excommunication does not take effect at all.

paragraphs: Nadar al daat chabero bishbil shum toba sheasa lo baabur shebua zo "p shechabero qibbel toba mehannishba yoter en mattirin lo ella middaat chabero veim met yesh mistappeqin im yoreshayv hem bimqomo latet reshut lehattir veim aberu vehittiru lo shello middaat chabero yesh omerim dimhanne hahattara bediabad veyesh omerim dela mehanne:

clarification.explanation: One who vowed based on his fellow's consent — that is, conditioned the vow on his fellow's agreement, due to some favor the fellow did for him — the vow is released only with that fellow's knowledge and consent, even though the fellow received a greater favor from the vower. And if the fellow died, some are in doubt whether his heirs step into his place to grant permission for release. And if the release was already granted without the fellow's knowledge, some say the release is effective after the fact and some say it is not effective.
takeaways: A vow made based on a fellow's consent is released only with that fellow's knowledge and consent.
If the fellow died, there is doubt whether his heirs step into his place.
Release granted without the fellow's knowledge is disputed whether effective after the fact.

paragraphs: En mattirin shum neder ushebua ad sheyyachul lepikak hannoder o nishba benisan shello yokal basar sheloshim yom min rosh chodesh iyyar en mattirin lo ella ad sheyyaggia rosh chodesh iyyar, veken im nishba o nadar sheyyitanneh besheni vachamishi vesheni - en mattirin lo ella ad sheyyaggia yom sheni harishon. bammeh debarim amurim? benishba o nadar beperush, deyesh kan neder o shebua min hattora abal al minhag bilbad shello nadar beperush deen kan chiyyub ella midderabbanan mattirin qodem sheyyachul ukemo shekkatab bet yeuddeh cheleq b siman tz"z:

clarification.explanation: No vow or oath is released until it actually takes effect. Therefore one who vows or swears in the month of Nissan not to eat meat for thirty days starting from the New Moon of Iyar is released only when the New Moon of Iyar arrives. Likewise, if he vowed or swore to fast on Mondays, Thursdays, and Mondays, he is released only when the first Monday arrives. This applies to one who explicitly vowed or swore, where there is a Torah-level vow or oath. But regarding a mere practice not explicitly vowed, whose obligation is only rabbinic, it is released even before it takes effect.
takeaways: No vow or oath is released until it actually takes effect.
A future vow is released only when the vow's time arrives.
This applies to an explicit, Torah-level vow or oath.
A mere rabbinic-level practice can be released even before it takes effect.

paragraphs: Teqiat kap dinah kishbua veyesh machmirin bah yoter velaken tzarik hattara, vehane mille keshehu oseh otah bederek qabbalat shebua, abal socharim shettoqein kappam zeh lazeh leqayyem hammiqqach en lazeh din shebua vehannishba bashshamayim veken benabi mehannebiim "p sheen lazeh day shebua gemura mikkol maqom tzarik lo hattara vehannishba bechayye napsho "g delekka bazeh issur shebua tzarik lizzaher shello yishshaba bechayye napsho vehaomer im yaaseh ken eno yehudi en zeh leshon shebua ak yesh bazeh issur gadol shehu debar chatziput neged haemuna vehaomerim beet shemmedabberim "debarim ellu emet kemo shhqb"h emet" hare zeh aon pelili vetzarik lizzaher bazeh meod;

clarification.explanation: A handshake, where a person extends his hand to his fellow to fulfill something, has the law of an oath, and some are even stricter about it, and it therefore requires release. This applies specifically when done as a form of accepting an oath, but merchants who shake hands to seal a deal — this has no oath status. One who swears by Heaven or by the name of one of the prophets, although this is not a full-fledged oath, nevertheless requires release. And one who swears by his own life, although this carries no oath prohibition, must be careful not to swear this way. And one who says "if he does so, he is not a Jew" — this is not oath-language, but it carries a great prohibition, being an act of impudence toward faith. And those who say in the course of their speech "these words are as true as the Holy One is true" commit a criminal transgression, and one must be very careful about this.
takeaways: A handshake as an oath-acceptance has the law of an oath and requires release; merchants' handshakes to seal a deal do not.
Swearing by Heaven or a prophet's name requires release even though not a full oath.
"If he does so, he is not a Jew" is not oath-language but carries a great prohibition.
Comparing one's words' truth to God's truth is a criminal transgression.

paragraphs: Mi shennishba shello yedabber im chabero yakol liktob lo ketab veken yakol ledabber im acher vehu shomea abal im nitkavven lehashmio "p sheyyesh echad benehem la arik lemebad haki:

clarification.explanation: One who swore not to speak with his fellow may write him a letter, and may also speak with another person while his fellow listens. But if he intended for his words to reach his fellow through that other person, even with a third person between them, it is not proper to do so, since this is circumventing his oath.
takeaways: One who swore not to speak with his fellow may write him a letter or speak to another while the fellow listens.
But intending to convey the message to the fellow through another person is improper circumvention of the oath.

paragraphs: Ishsha nadera shebbekol yeme ibbur shellah tadliq beyadah ner bebet hakkeneset bekol shabbat veachar shehitchila bedabar zeh shalosh vearba shabbatot tericha lah milleta lelek kol ereb shabbat lebet hakkeneset lehadliq verotzeh lehadliq arba nerot beshabbat echad baabur kol arba shabbatot gam od rotzeh lelek lzyyr"h bispina, vetihyeh beshabbat bispina ketzad taaseh heeleti bs"d bsh"q rab pealim deenah rashshaa lehadliq nerot arba shabbatot beshabbat echad ubeotah shabbat shehi bispina taaseh shalicha bimqomah lehadliq baaburah:

clarification.explanation: A woman who vowed that throughout her pregnancy she would light a candle by hand in the synagogue every Sabbath, and after beginning this for three or four Sabbaths, it became burdensome for her to go to the synagogue every Sabbath eve, and she wishes to light four candles on one Sabbath for all four Sabbaths, and also wishes to travel by ship to visit the graves of the righteous and will be on the ship on a Sabbath. The author of the Ben Ish Chai raised in his book Rav Pe'alim that she may not light the candles of four Sabbaths on one Sabbath, but must light on each Sabbath at its proper time. On the Sabbath she is on the ship, she should appoint an agent to light the candle in her place.
takeaways: One who vowed to light a candle every Sabbath may not light several candles on one Sabbath for multiple Sabbaths.
The vow requires lighting on each Sabbath at its proper time.
On a Sabbath she is prevented (such as being on a ship), she should appoint an agent to light in her place.

paragraphs: Qatan ben y"b shana veyom echad uqetanna bat y" shana veyom echad im yodein leshem mi naderu venishbeu nidram ushebuatam qayyamin vekannizkar beshulchan aruk mihu leinyan sheela im yekolim lehattir lahem o lav haaleti bsh"q rab pealim desapeq zeh nistappequ bo haacharonim velo nipshat veazelinan beh lechumera veayyen mishneh lammelek bepereq b' mehilkot gezerot vechiqre leb yoreh dea cheleq b' siman s' veshaot derabbanan dap n' vezakur leabraham abigedor eben haezer siman d' dap l' yeuyyan sham:

clarification.explanation: A minor boy who is twelve years and a day old, and a minor girl who is eleven years and a day old, who are in the year approaching maturity, if they know for whose sake they vowed and swore, their vow and oath are valid, as mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch. But regarding whether their vows can be released, the author of the Ben Ish Chai raised in his book Rav Pe'alim that this doubt was left unresolved by the later authorities, and therefore one is stringent about it.
takeaways: A boy of twelve years and a day, and a girl of eleven years and a day, have valid vows if they know for whose sake they vowed.
These are "mufla samukh l'ish" vows, in the year before maturity.
Regarding releasing their vows, the doubt is unresolved, and one is stringent.

paragraphs: Hamqabbel taanit meammud hashshachar tob sheyyatneh qodem sheyyashen beperush sheyyishteh mayim vqhvv"y (qph) beashmoret qodem ammud hashshachar achar hashshena v"g deyesh omerim damim muttar apillu bistam deeno meparesh mihu al akila la mehanne tenay sheyyokal achar sheyyashen shinat qeba shello veim shakach leqabbel taanit bishat mincha venizkar ben hashshemashot qodem shehitpallel arbit heeleti bsh"q rab pealim sheyyeqabbel taanit ben hashshemashot veomer anenu veayyen mishbetzot zahab siman tqs"b beresh hassiman:

clarification.explanation: One who undertakes a fast from dawn should preferably explicitly stipulate before sleeping that he be permitted to drink water and coffee during the early morning watch before dawn after waking. Although some say water is permitted even without an explicit condition, nevertheless for eating, the condition does not help, and he cannot eat after a proper night's sleep. And if he forgot to accept the fast at the Minchah prayer and remembered at twilight before praying the evening service, the author of the Ben Ish Chai raised in his book Rav Pe'alim that he should accept the fast at twilight and say "Aneinu" in his prayer.
takeaways: One undertaking a dawn fast should stipulate permission to drink water and coffee in the early morning before dawn.
The condition does not help for eating after a proper night's sleep.
Forgetting to accept the fast at Minchah, remembered at twilight — accept it then and say "Aneinu."

paragraphs: Haab meper nidre bitto kol zeman shehi qetanna o naara apillu nadera al daat rabbim abal im nisset qodem zeman zeh eno yakol lehaper vehu haddin im bagera deeno yakol lehaper veniqret qetanna ad y"b veyom echad ubat y"b shana veyom echad niqret naara ad shishsha chodashim veachar y"b shana veshishsha chodashim niqret bogeret vehabbaal meper nidre ishto lebaddo mishshettikkanes lachuppa ad shettitgaresh veyaggia hagget leyadah velav davqa nedarim ella hu haddin shebuot name meperin haab vehabbaal kedin nedarim vekamporash bedibre haramba"m ubedibre maran za"l umah shekkatab hakkeneset haggedola behaggahat hattur ot Adonai kebar amad al debarayv haggaon chida" za"l bebirke yosep siman rl"d:

clarification.explanation: A father annuls his daughter's vows as long as she is a minor or a "na'arah" (an adolescent), even if she vowed with the intent of many. But if she married before then, the father cannot annul, and likewise if she reached full maturity ("bogeret"), he cannot annul. She is called a minor until age twelve years and a day, and from twelve years and a day she is called a "na'arah" for six months, and after twelve years and six months she is called a "bogeret." And the husband alone annuls his wife's vows, from the time she enters the wedding canopy until she is divorced and the divorce document reaches her hand. And not only vows, but the father and husband also annul oaths, following the law of vows.
takeaways: A father annuls his daughter's vows while she is a minor or a na'arah.
Marriage or reaching bogeret status ends the father's power to annul.
A na'arah spans age twelve years and a day, for six months; afterward she is a bogeret.
The husband annuls his wife's vows (and oaths) from the wedding until divorce is finalized.

paragraphs: En haab vehabbaal yekolin lehaper ella raq bayyom shomeam veim shameu ballayla yekolin lehaper kol hallayla vekol yom hammachorat veim shameu samuk lachasheka en meperin ella ad shettechshak veim shatequ velo happiro "p shebbelibbam lehaper veraq shatequ kede letzaarah - kol sheabar yom shomeam en yekolim lehaper od. mihu im lo heper mechamat chesron yedia sheeno yada sheyyesh lo koach lehaper hare zeh yakol lehaper bayyom sheshshama haddin hazzeh apillu achar hanneder vehashshebua bekamma yamim veyihyeh yom yediato din zeh keyom shameu sheyyesh lo zeman lehaper ad sop hayyom:

clarification.explanation: The father and husband can only annul the vow on the day they heard it. If they heard it at night, they may annul throughout that night and the following day. If they heard it close to nightfall, they may annul only until it becomes dark. And if they remained silent and did not annul, even if in their heart they intended to annul and only remained silent to distress her, once the day of hearing has passed, they can no longer annul. But if he did not annul because he did not know he had the power to annul, he may annul on the day he learns of this law, even several days after the vow, and the day he learns the law is considered for him as the day of hearing, giving him until its end to annul.
takeaways: The father and husband may annul only on the day they heard the vow (or the following day if heard at night).
Heard close to nightfall — may annul only until dark.
Remaining silent through the day of hearing forfeits the power to annul.
Not annulling due to ignorance of the law — he may annul on the day he learns of it.

paragraphs: Ketzad hahapara yomar lah mupar liki shelosh peamim kede lechazzeq haddabar mihu bepaam achat name have hapara veken bahaqama bepaam achat name sheamar lah qayyam liki have haqama veeno yakol lehaper achar haqamato veim amar lah batel liki o amar leh in neder zeh kelum chashib leshon hapara vehu haddin im amar lah hahapara bishar leshonot asher mashmautam hapara dimhanne vehu haddin beinyan hahaqama abal im amar lah i ipshi shettaduri, o amar lah en kan neder - en zeh leshon hapara vela mehanne, mihu im belibbo chashab leshon hapara velo hotzi bispatayv ella raq amar lah tulle veakeli kevan dechashab leshon hahapara belibbo veamar ken bepiv mehanne vehinneh yesh debarim sheyyukal lehaper veyesh shello yukal lehaper, al ken habbaal al kol panim yaper beyom shameu veaach"k yishal lehammoreh veyaggid lo hahalaka vetabo alayv beraka:

clarification.explanation: How the annulment is performed: the husband or father says to her "annulled for you" three times to strengthen the matter, but even once effects the annulment. Likewise for confirming a vow, if he said to her once "confirmed for you," this is a confirmation, and he can no longer annul after confirming. And if he said to her "voided for you," or said "this vow is nothing," this is considered annulment language, and likewise any language meaning annulment is effective, and the same for confirmation. But if he said to her "I do not wish you to vow" or "there is no vow here," this is not annulment language and is not effective. Nevertheless, if he thought annulment language in his heart but did not utter it with his lips, only saying to her "take and eat," since he thought annulment language in his heart and spoke accordingly with his mouth, the annulment is effective. And since there are things he can annul and things he cannot, in any case the husband should annul on the day he heard it, and afterward ask a halachic authority to tell him the law, and blessing will come upon him.
takeaways: Annulment is stated "annulled for you," customarily three times though once suffices.
Confirmation is "confirmed for you" — after confirming, he can no longer annul.
"Voided for you" or "this vow is nothing" are effective annulment language; "I do not wish you to vow" is not.
In any case, the husband should annul on the day he heard it, then consult a halachic authority afterward.
